ev.chn_fc_bazi.ugly.ok: So at home they called you Dog's Leftovers. Grandmother swears no spirit would want a thing like that.
ev.chn_fc_bazi.temple.ok: You were carried to the monastery, where the monks wrote you into their book and gave you a "temple name". Now you belong to them a little - and the Buddha, they say, will keep watch.
ev.chn_fc_bazi.refuse.ok: Your father pressed a copper into the fortune-teller's hand and saw him out: "Everyone in our family is sturdy." Grandmother later slipped an extra stick of incense before the ancestral tablets.
ev.chn_fc_bazi.title: The eight characters
ev.chn_fc_bazi.text: Your father called in a fortune-teller, who laid out your eight characters on the table - the year, month, day and hour of your birth, two signs for each. His face fell: "Plenty of fire, no water at all - this child will be hard to raise." He advises giving you a deliberately ugly milk name, so that evil spirits turn up their noses, or "registering" you with a Buddhist monastery under the Buddha's protection.
ev.chn_fc_bazi.note: Fortune-telling by the "eight characters" (bazi) - the cyclical signs of the year, month, day and hour of birth - took shape by the Song period. If a child's fate came out "heavy", it was given a deliberately ugly milk name - Dog's Leftovers, Stone, Iron Egg - or "given in name" to a monastery so that the gods would protect it.
ev.chn_fc_bazi_nickname.title: Dog's Leftovers
ev.chn_fc_bazi_nickname.text: For years the neighbourhood children teased you about your milk name - and then smallpox went down the lane, and you were the only one it spared. Grandmother is triumphant: "What spirit would bother with Leftovers!" Since then you say your nickname with pride.
ev.chn_fc_bazi_temple.title: Temple characters
ev.chn_fc_bazi_temple.text: The monks who wrote you into their book as a baby invited you to the Bathing of the Buddha festival and did not let you go empty-handed: an old monk took it on himself to teach you characters. You copied sutras until your wrist ached - and now you can read every shop sign in the street.
ev.chn_fc_baijia.scraps.ok: Your mother went round the whole quarter and nobody refused: one gave a scrap of silk, another a strip of blue homespun. The robe came out as motley as a magpie's nest, and now the neighbours think of you as a little bit theirs.
ev.chn_fc_baijia.lock.ok: The silversmith cast a tiny lock inscribed "long life". It hung round your neck on a red cord and tinkled whenever anyone picked you up.
ev.chn_fc_baijia.none.ok: "The child will grow up anyway," the household decided. Grandmother sighed and tied a red thread round your wrist - better than nothing.
ev.chn_fc_baijia.title: The hundred-family robe
ev.chn_fc_baijia.text: Grandmother says that for a child to live long, it must borrow luck from many families. Your mother could go round the neighbours and beg a scrap of cloth from each - a hundred scraps make a "hundred-family robe". Or you could order a silver "longevity lock" from the silversmith to hang round your neck: it locks life inside the body, and no spirit can drag it away.
ev.chn_fc_baijia.note: The "hundred-family robe" (baijia yi) and the "longevity lock" (changming suo) were children's charms: scraps from many families were thought to lend the child their luck, and the little silver lock to lock life inside it. Both customs are well known from the Ming and Qing periods; exactly when they began is hard to say.
ev.chn_fc_baijia_lantern.title: A hundred families
ev.chn_fc_baijia_lantern.text: At the Lantern Festival you fell behind your family and got lost in the crowd. Within the hour a tofu seller brought you home: "This one's ours - from the hundred-family robe!" Your mother laughed and cried at once, and the neighbours retold the story for a week.
ev.chn_fc_baijia_pawn.title: The lock at the pawnshop
ev.chn_fc_baijia_pawn.text: It was a hungry year, and you yourself took to the pawnshop the silver longevity lock that hung round your neck as a baby. The owner, behind his high counter, weighed it and gave a good price. A pity to part with it - but it seems the lock has already locked your life in safely.
